summary: Knechtle offered cumulative historical, moral, and experiential support for Christianity; Dillahunty prevailed by demanding stronger links from reports and effects to supernatural conclusions.

pro-limited-evidence-preserves-free-trus.description: Knechtle argues that God provides sufficient intellectual and affective evidence for freely chosen trust, whereas undeniable manifestation would secure only assent, not relationship.
pro-limited-evidence-preserves-free-trus.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle directly confronts Dillahunty’s communicative-God challenge by distinguishing propositional assent from voluntarily relational trust, while Matthew 28 suggests physical encounter need not produce enduring belief. Principal limitation: Neither the claim that resurrection witnesses soon abandoned belief nor “just enough evidence” establishes an assessable threshold; moreover, clearer disclosure is characterized as coercive without addressing intermediate possibilities or nonresistant uncertainty. Live burden: Knechtle must demonstrate that Christianity’s intellectual and affective indicators are sufficient, explain why stronger yet resistible evidence would damage freely chosen relationship, and connect his disciples comparison to divine hiddenness. Locked score: 70 rewards direct engagement and substantial motion-level relevance, while weak evidential grounding, undefined calibration, and incomplete contact with Dillahunty’s objection keep this coherent distinction from establishing Christianity’s rationality.

con-rationality-requires-reality-consist.description: By comparing coherent fictional rule systems with actual belief, Dillahunty argues that rationality demands more than internal consistency: claims must fit reality’s facts.
con-rationality-requires-reality-consist.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s Mario and Dungeons and Dragons comparisons sharply expose the inferential gap between coherence under invented rules and rational warrant about an external world, fixing the motion’s epistemic standard. Principal limitation: Those examples demonstrate that internal consistency is insufficient, but they neither specify which factual correspondence counts nor establish that Christianity fails it, while “irrelevant” understates coherence’s screening role. Live burden: He must supply a defensible test distinguishing mere compatibility with reality from evidential confirmation, then apply that test to Christianity rather than leaving the external comparison implicit. Locked score: 84 appropriately reflects exceptional burden relevance and responsiveness, strong clarity and coherence, but only moderate evidential support and slightly compressed calibration in the positive reality-based standard.

pro-multifaceted-return-to-faith.description: Knechtle presents his return to Christianity as the result of accumulated evidence and rejecting hedonism as bankrupt, thereby asserting that faith had rational warrant.
pro-multifaceted-return-to-faith.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle’s first-person sequence—rejecting hedonism’s “bankruptcy,” then returning after seeing “all this evidence”—intelligibly challenges Dillahunty’s claim that Christianity lacks warrant. Principal limitation: Neither the evidence nor hedonism’s alleged inadequacy is specified, and abandoning hedonism does not establish Christianity; consequently, it never meets Dillahunty’s reality-consistency test or demand for verifiable support. Live burden: Knechtle must identify the considerations, explain how they connect rejection of hedonism to Christian belief, and demonstrate why they remain assessable beyond the private force of his conversion experience. Locked score: 64 recognizes clear autobiographical structure, measured personal framing, reply contact, and motion relevance, while reserving substantial credit because the decisive evidence is unauditable here, the comparative inference is incomplete, and the opponent’s evidential standard remains unanswered.

con-communicative-god-leaves-burden-unme.description: Dillahunty argues that Christianity’s allegedly communicative God has not delivered verifiable support or a justifying explanation, so Christianity has not discharged its rational burden.
con-communicative-god-leaves-burden-unme.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty turns God’s claimed communicative capacity into an evidential expectation and connects its alleged nonfulfillment directly to rational withholding, yielding unusually strong responsiveness and motion-level burden relevance. Principal limitation: Although the excerpt says Christian claims lack “evidence or verifiable observation,” it neither examines the proffered evidence nor defends why divine communication should produce Dillahunty’s particular public, falsifiable model. Live burden: He must specify what adequate disclosure would involve, justify the expectation from God’s capacities, and demonstrate that disputed experiences and arguments genuinely fail that standard. Locked score: A 78 appropriately rewards the intelligible inference and exceptionally direct debate contact while withholding credit because the pivotal absence claim is asserted broadly, with limited precision and charitable engagement.

con-evidentiary-warrant-can-differ-by-pe.description: Dillahunty argues that rational belief tracks each person’s available evidence, so the same objectively true proposition may warrant belief for one person but not another.
con-evidentiary-warrant-can-differ-by-pe.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty sharply separates objective truth from person-relative rational warrant: God could exist, reveal himself convincingly to Knechtle, withhold comparable evidence from Dillahunty, and thereby rationally differentiate their beliefs. Principal limitation: This hypothetical demonstrates conceptual possibility, not either participant’s actual evidence, while leaving the evidential threshold distinguishing justified acceptance from irrational belief materially underdeveloped. Live burden: Dillahunty must identify which publicly assessable or privately accessible considerations justify withholding his belief, explain how conflicting revelations should be evaluated, and connect that account to his central reality test. Locked score: The 86 properly rewards exceptional calibration, inferential coherence, precise exposition, and relevant clarification while preserving an evidentiary discount because the example maps possible unequal access more convincingly than it establishes anyone’s actual warrant.

pro-jesus-claims-divinity.description: Knechtle argues that the Gospels portray Jesus as divine through John's seven I-am sayings, his acceptance of worship, and his asserted authority to forgive sins.
pro-jesus-claims-divinity.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle's cumulative inference unites John's seven I-am sayings, Jesus's acceptance of worship unlike apostles and angels, and forgiveness authority, making a divine Gospel portrayal intelligible and directly relevant. Principal limitation: He supplies no passages, never establishes that these features uniquely indicate divinity, and generalizes from selected examples to Gospel-wide consistency while collapsing explicit self-identification into interpreted prerogative. Live burden: He must defend the divine interpretation against plausible alternatives, substantiate its scope across the Gospels, and connect narrative portrayal to Christianity's truth and rational warrant. Locked score: A 77 credits coherent, responsive use of concrete Gospel motifs while reserving points for absent citations, uncertain interpretive exclusivity, imprecise scope, and the unfinished transition from portrayal to warranted belief.

con-report-cannot-establish-forgiveness.description: Dillahunty argues that a preserved Gospel report alone establishes neither Jesus’s unity with the Father nor the occurrence and efficacy of supernatural forgiveness.
con-report-cannot-establish-forgiveness.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty isolates the equivocation between transmission of a report and establishment of its supernatural content, answering Knechtle’s manuscript defense and appeal to Jesus forgiving sins. Principal limitation: Although “provide evidence to show that this happened” identifies the missing warrant, the reply never explains what evidence could demonstrate whether a sin was genuinely forgiven or establish Jesus’s relation to the Father. Live burden: He must articulate criteria for moving from testimony to theological actuality, then show why manuscript abundance, early dating, and patristic quotation cannot meet them without treating testimony as worthless. Locked score: The 86 reflects exceptional responsiveness and strong coherence, relevance, clarity, and charity, while weaker evidential warrant preserves the unresolved challenge of specifying confirmatory evidence for forgiveness itself.

pro-gospel-transmission-reliability.description: Knechtle argues that abundant manuscripts, early dates, patristic quotations, and decentralized custody make coordinated alteration implausible, thereby supporting the Gospel text's reliability.
pro-gospel-transmission-reliability.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle's 5,800 manuscripts, more than one million patristic quotations, and decentralized custody directly resist coordinated alteration, materially advancing the subsidiary Gospel-reliability bridge with unusually concrete transmission considerations. Principal limitation: His quantities remain unsourced, "dates within 15 years" has no clear referent, and neither manuscript age, witness dependence, nor textual variation is examined, leaving preservation distinct from historical accuracy. Live burden: Because this constructive anticipates alteration objections rather than answering a specific reply, Knechtle must substantiate his chronology and counts, then show that decentralized preservation makes transmitted testimony credible about events. Locked score: The 69 appropriately rewards strong responsiveness and burden relevance while discounting weak sourcing, conceptual slippage, and the overconfident claim that contrary alteration accounts lack merit.

con-historical-evidence-can-be-source-st.description: Dillahunty treats past reports as gradable evidence, arguing that agreement among numerous genuinely competing sources increases confidence when direct empirical verification is unavailable.
con-historical-evidence-can-be-source-st.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s answer makes his testimony standard comparative rather than dismissive, expressly admitting reports from the empirically inaccessible past while explaining why concordance between numerous competing parties increases confidence. Principal limitation: The example never establishes that Gospel accounts are independent, adversarial, or insulated from common traditions, and his self-correction leaves provenance, genre, and reporter reliability insufficiently specified. Live burden: To reinforce his testimony objection, Dillahunty must apply these criteria to debated sources, distinguish numerical plurality from evidential independence, and demonstrate whether cross-party consistency materially improves Christianity’s warrant. Locked score: 82 appropriately rewards the coherent qualification, direct answer, source comparison, and charitable calibration, while comparatively weaker precision and evidential support reflect missing Gospel-level application and unresolved dependence questions.

pro-resurrection-cumulative-indicia.description: Knechtle argues that witness reports, skeptical conversions, immediate proclamation, the empty tomb, costly adherence, and rapid church formation jointly make the resurrection historically credible.
pro-resurrection-cumulative-indicia.critique: Strongest feature: As an opening constructive without reply contact, Knechtle combines witness reports, skeptical conversions, immediate proclamation, an empty tomb, costly adherence, and rapid ecclesial emergence into a cumulative inference addressing Christianity’s supernatural center. Principal limitation: The span enumerates categories without providing underlying sources, chronological corroboration, independence analysis, or a discriminating comparison demonstrating why their conjunction favors bodily resurrection over naturalistic alternatives. Live burden: Since conviction, suffering, proclamation, and institutional growth can accompany mistaken beliefs, Knechtle must establish each premise’s reliability and show that their combined pattern becomes likelier if resurrection occurred. Locked score: Seventy-four appropriately rewards a coherent, relevant constructive whose inventory engages the motion, while withholding credit because evidential foundations, comparative testing, causal linkage, and the “overnight” characterization remain underdeveloped.

con-supernatural-claims-undemonstrated.description: Dillahunty argues that Christianity’s unverified and untestable supernatural claims cannot rationally support its explanations, because elaborating a miracle cannot substitute for demonstrating it occurred.
con-supernatural-claims-undemonstrated.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly contests Knechtle’s cumulative indicia by separating historical considerations from demonstration that resurrection occurred, and an alleged occurrence from a warranted supernatural explanation. Principal limitation: The fairy comparison illuminates explanation-before-establishment, but categorical claims that no Christian supernatural claim has ever been demonstrated and that Christianity contradicts reality remain unsupported, while testability, falsifiability, occurrence, and explanatory warrant blur together. Live burden: He must show why the witnesses, conversions, empty tomb, proclamation, costly adherence, and early-church emergence collectively fail to verify resurrection, while defending his proposed evidential requirements. Locked score: 77 appropriately rewards unusually direct central-burden contact, coherent verification-before-explanation reasoning, and clear responsiveness, while reduced evidential warrant and calibration register unsupported universals and insufficiently defended methodology.

pro-six-source-resurrection-reply.description: Knechtle argues that six resurrection sources form a multifaceted historical case stronger than the thinner sourcing often accepted for ancient events and directly challenge Dillahunty's single-story objection.
pro-six-source-resurrection-reply.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle directly answers Dillahunty’s claim that resurrection testimony is merely a story by presenting six sources and situating their multiplicity within ordinary historical reasoning. Principal limitation: He neither identifies those sources nor examines their independence, dating, access, agreement, or reliability, while his two-source comparison misleadingly treats unequal reports and extraordinary events as evidentially interchangeable. Live burden: Source quantity must still establish genuinely independent confirmation of the resurrection itself, rather than repeated preservation of a claim, and then connect that event to forgiveness or divine causation. Locked score: The 67 appropriately reflects strong relevance and direct contact with the single-story objection, alongside middling evidential warrant, imprecise historical standards, and an overconfident inference from numerical multiplicity.

con-scriptural-story-is-not-miracle-evid.description: Dillahunty argues that New Testament miracle narratives, including the resurrection, merely report supernatural claims and cannot independently establish those claims as true.
con-scriptural-story-is-not-miracle-evid.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty sharply distinguishes faithfully transmitting resurrection and healing narratives from independently confirming their supernatural contents, directly confronting Knechtle’s manuscript-reliability argument and cumulative resurrection indicia. Principal limitation: His categorical assertion that a story is not evidence unjustifiably collapses potentially limited testimonial evidence into evidential nullity, without examining provenance, source independence, corroboration, or Knechtle’s cumulative presentation. Live burden: He still must demonstrate why the cited witness reports, conversions, empty tomb, immediate proclamation, costly adherence, and early-church emergence collectively remain insufficient, rather than relying exclusively on the report-event distinction. Locked score: The score of 78 appropriately rewards direct reply contact, lucid burden relevance, and coherent resistance to textual self-validation, while withholding credit because evidential warrant and charitable calibration lag behind responsiveness and precision.

con-observed-effect-needs-causal-link.description: Dillahunty argues that even witnessing a severed finger regrow would leave divine agency unproven until evidence connected that extraordinary result specifically to God.
con-observed-effect-needs-causal-link.critique: Strongest feature: By adopting Knechtle's laboratory example, Dillahunty sharply separates verification of finger regrowth from identification of its cause, granting that God remains possible while explaining why neither an extraordinary observation nor six historical sources supplies discriminating evidence of divine agency. Principal limitation: The hypothetical clarifies the inferential standard rather than applying it to the resurrection record, and it leaves unspecified what observable evidence could distinguish divine action from unknown natural causation or other proposed explanations. Live burden: Dillahunty must show cumulative indicia and multiple reports establish only an alleged anomaly without independently bridging it to God, while specifying a workable test for his demanded linkage. Locked score: 88 fits the exceptional burden contact and responsiveness, tempered by comparatively weaker evidential warrant.

pro-christianity-explains-altruism-hope.description: Knechtle argues that Christianity better explains costly out-group concern, sacrificial love, and enduring hope than an evolutionary picture he portrays as naturally violent.
pro-christianity-explains-altruism-hope.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle identifies sympathy, sacrificial love, aid to outsiders, and persistent hope, giving this experiential-fit case constructive responsiveness and substantial motion relevance without replying to opposition. Principal limitation: His excerpt asserts Judeo-Christian cultural causation and portrays evolution as naturally violent, offering neither historical corroboration nor engagement with evolutionary cooperation, while leaving hope's connection to eternal reality underdetermined. Live burden: He must show that costly out-group concern resists natural explanation, distinguish Christianity's superiority from cultural influence or psychological usefulness, and justify why durable hope indicates a specifically Christian eternal reality. Locked score: The 59 reflects the frozen unevenness: strong relevance and constructive contact sustain the argument, but thin evidence, incomplete comparison, imprecise causation, and an uncharitable evolutionary contrast substantially restrain its force.

con-natural-account-of-cooperation.description: Dillahunty argues that secular humanists need not presume innate goodness because shared problems and strategic interdependence can generate cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness without Christianity.
con-natural-account-of-cooperation.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly confronts Knechtle’s explanatory claim by separating secular humanism from presumed innate goodness and presenting strategic interdependence as an intelligible alternative source of cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness. Principal limitation: Invoking “properly applied Game Theory” identifies a relevant framework but supplies neither a concrete mechanism nor comparative evidence showing how reciprocal problem-solving extends to costly out-group concern, sacrificial conduct, sympathy, or forgiveness. Live burden: The rebuttal must demonstrate that strategic interdependence explains the morally demanding phenomena Knechtle emphasized, rather than merely establishing that cooperation can emerge without religious commitment. Locked score: 77 appropriately reflects unusually strong reply contact and substantial relevance while discounting the compressed mechanism, absent examples, and overbroad assertion that these virtues are not Christian functions at all.

pro-jesus-transformed-roman-morality.description: By contrasting normalized Roman slavery, sexual license, and inequality with Jesus-inspired egalitarian change, Knechtle argues that Christianity exerted a distinctive and rationally significant historical influence.
pro-jesus-transformed-roman-morality.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle’s concrete juxtaposition of normalized Roman slavery, sexual license, and inequality against Jesus-associated egalitarian transformation challenges Dillahunty’s contention that cooperation, sympathy, and forgiveness emerge through secular problem-solving and game-theoretic interdependence. Principal limitation: The vivid contrast supplies neither chronology, representative Roman sources, comparison groups, nor causal discrimination between Christian teaching and gradual non-Christian developments, so asserted influence cannot establish Jesus’s divinity or Christianity’s rational truth. Live burden: Show why these changes were specifically caused by Jesus’s movement, distinguish that explanation from secular and competing historical causes, and connect influence to supernatural warrant. Locked score: Sixty rewards a coherent, relevant reply with genuine contact, while middling evidential support and sweeping Roman generalizations prevent the claimed transformation from carrying the central rationality burden.

con-social-benefit-does-not-warrant-supe.description: Dillahunty grants for argument’s sake that Christianity might produce a better society, yet denies that such results justify believing its central supernatural doctrines.
con-social-benefit-does-not-warrant-supe.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty’s concession directly meets Knechtle’s appeals to altruism, hope, and transformed Roman morality while isolating the inference’s defect: desirable social consequences do not authenticate supernatural propositions. Principal limitation: The reply states rather than develops its epistemic principle, and the excerpt never specifies which supernatural claims require independent support or why pragmatic success could not contribute to their plausibility. Live burden: Having neutralized benefit as sufficient warrant without disputing the alleged benefits, Dillahunty still must assess historical or experiential evidence Knechtle offers for Jesus’s divinity and Christianity’s distinctive truth. Locked score: Ninety fits the coherent, charitable, motion-level reply and its decisive contact with both opposing moves, while the lower evidential showing reflects an asserted distinction whose implications are not defended.

con-religious-desire-does-not-show-truth.description: Religious longing and facts merely compatible with Christianity provide no support unless a demonstrable link connects Christianity’s explanation to the experiences or facts invoked.
con-religious-desire-does-not-show-truth.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly answers Knechtle’s appeal to hope and religious fulfillment by distinguishing observations consistent with Christianity from evidence that specifically connects those observations to Christianity’s explanatory account. Principal limitation: His claim that non-falsifiability makes evidence impossible overstates the methodological point, while assertions that human invention explains every religion and Christianity has zero support receive no defense here. Live burden: The reply needs an articulated account of what evidential connection would discriminate Christianity from natural explanations, especially if Knechtle argues cumulative experiential fit supplies probabilistic rather than demonstrative support. Locked score: 80 appropriately reflects exceptional reply contact and burden relevance alongside a coherent compatibility-versus-evidence distinction, while reserving credit for the move’s unsupported universality, compressed epistemology, and insufficiently charitable scope.

pro-love-and-wrath-are-coherent.description: Knechtle argues that protective opposition to harm can express love, so divine wrath need not conflict with love and may prevent moral indifference.
pro-love-and-wrath-are-coherent.critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle explains the contradiction through protective love: opposition to whatever harms a person can express care, while indifference toward wrongdoing would betray it, supporting coherent divine character. Principal limitation: The analogy establishes possibility, not application: no divine punishment is shown to be protective, proportionate, or just, and “a type of Wrath” leaves loving resistance indistinct from punitive violence. Live burden: Since this constructive addresses an anticipated tension rather than an identified opposing move, Knechtle must connect loving anger to contested punishments and demonstrate that they reliably oppose harm without creating harm. Locked score: The mid-seventies outcome reflects stronger coherence, responsiveness, and burden relevance than evidential warrant or calibration, especially because “couldn’t be any more consistent” overstates this comparison.

con-biblical-violence-challenges-charact.description: Dillahunty cites the flood, firstborn deaths, Babel, hell, and Jesus’s temple scourge to challenge whether Knechtle can coherently reconcile divine wrath with love.
con-biblical-violence-challenges-charact.critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly tests Knechtle’s claim that loving wrath opposes harm by citing the flood, firstborn deaths, Babel, hell, and the temple scourge as apparent counterexamples requiring explanation. Principal limitation: The compressed catalogue supplies no textual context, conflates distinct divine actions, misstates Babel as destruction, and leaves “sentence everyone to Hell by default” doctrinally undefended, while sarcasm reduces charitable engagement. Live burden: He must show that cited victims are not relevant wrongdoers, establish morally comparable features across episodes, and defeat contextual reconciliations grounded in justice. Locked score: 77 appropriately rewards direct reply contact, concrete scriptural touchpoints, coherent counterexample pressure, and substantial relevance to divine-character tension, while withholding credit because evidential underdevelopment and rhetorical overreach prevent the catalogue from establishing incoherence.

con-forgiveness-and-hell-undermine-justi.description: Dillahunty argues that forgiving a mass murderer while eternally punishing victims disconnects ultimate outcomes from proportional desert, undermining Knechtle’s reconciliation of divine love and wrath.
con-forgiveness-and-hell-undermine-justi.critique: Strongest feature: The murderer-victim reversal directly engages Knechtle’s contention that wrath prevents indifference toward wrongdoing, because forgiving the perpetrator while eternally punishing victims makes ultimate outcomes appear disconnected from proportional desert. Principal limitation: Dillahunty presents a doctrinal hypothetical without establishing that Knechtle’s theology assigns either destiny as alleged, while calling Christian justice a bizarre lie, grossly immoral, and embarrassing greatly exceeds the argument’s compressed support. Live burden: He must specify how repentance, belief, culpability, forgiveness, and further judgment determine both destinies, then show that doctrinal qualifications cannot restore proportionate justice. Locked score: The score of 76 fits an exceptionally responsive, burden-relevant challenge with a lucid contrast, while discounting unverified assumptions, incomplete specification, and uncharitable certainty.

strengths: Knechtle assembled a genuinely cumulative case spanning Gospel portrayal, textual transmission, resurrection traditions, moral transformation, human hope, and divine-character coherence.
His replies repeatedly contacted Dillahunty’s objections, especially through free relational trust, multiple resurrection sources, and Christianity’s claimed countercultural moral influence.
The case identified substantial explananda—including costly altruism, religious hope, rapid movement growth, and protective wrath—that merit comparative worldview explanation.
blunders: Textual preservation and reported divine claims were repeatedly treated as historical or supernatural truth without supplying the necessary evidential and causal bridges.
Manuscript counts, dating claims, patristic quotations, and resurrection-source totals remained unsourced, ambiguously defined, and largely untested for genuine independence.
Evolutionary and moral comparisons overstated Christian uniqueness, underdescribed natural alternatives, and confused beneficial social influence with evidence for supernatural doctrine.

strengths: Dillahunty consistently distinguished internal coherence, factual occurrence, evidential warrant, and causal identification across the debate’s historical, experiential, and moral disputes.
His best replies granted reports, anomalies, or social benefits provisionally, then exposed why those facts still would not independently identify supernatural causes.

He allowed person-relative warrant and nonempirical historical evidence, identifying multiplicity, independence, competing provenance, and corroboration as legitimate evidential strengthening conditions.
blunders: Testability and falsifiability were sometimes presented as universal requirements for rational belief without sufficient defense regarding historical or metaphysical propositions.
Categorical claims that stories are not evidence obscured the more defensible distinction between testimony possessing some weight and testimony remaining insufficient.

Divine-character objections compressed contested doctrinal assumptions and used adversarial overstatement, weakening serious concerns about proportionality, forgiveness, violence, and eternal punishment.

finalArgument.thesis: Christianity is rationally warranted when, taken together, early historical testimony, transformative effects, moral experience, and a coherent account of divine character explain the evidence better than considered alternatives, while remaining defeasible.
premises: Because early testimony can be historically recoverable, it offers defeasible evidence that Jesus was regarded as divine and that followers sincerely proclaimed his resurrection, without independently proving either claim.

Because empty-tomb traditions, conversions, costly adherence, immediate proclamation, and rapid movement emergence form a convergent pattern, resurrection may fit them better than multiple independently stipulated natural explanations.

Christian teaching encouraged countercultural equality, forgiveness, sacrificial concern, and hope; insofar as these outcomes were distinctive and costly, they modestly support a personally and morally purposive reality.

Limited public manifestation may preserve voluntary relational trust rather than compelled assent, while converging historical, experiential, and moral evidence can still give responsible inquirers sufficient grounds for commitment.

Protective divine wrath can be compatible with love when it proportionately opposes genuine harm, imposes just accountability, and leaves wrongdoers a meaningful path toward forgiveness and restoration.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because these partially independent considerations mutually reinforce one another without depending on any single decisive proof, Christian commitment can be rationally justified, provided each strand is weighted by its reliability and surviving defeaters.

newArguments.title: Comparative cumulative likelihood
newArguments.text: Knechtle could compare how probable each historical, moral, and experiential observation would be under Christianity and specific naturalistic alternatives, rather than merely listing considerations. The comparison should separate independent evidence from repeated reports of the same source, state contested premises openly, and weight each strand according to its provenance and reliability. He could then ask whether their combined likelihood ratio favors resurrection and theism, while testing sensitivity to disputed assumptions and conceding that modest cumulative support does not make any single observation demonstrative of a miracle.

newArguments.title: Public and private warrant
newArguments.text: The defense could distinguish a public evidential baseline from person-specific experiential warrant. Historical testimony and publicly assessable arguments would supply reasons available to any investigator, while conscience, moral transformation, or an apparent encounter could rationally increase one person's confidence only after scrutiny for sincerity, reliability, alternative explanations, and defeating evidence. This distinction builds on Dillahunty's concession that warrant can vary by person, yet it preserves epistemic modesty: inaccessible experiences may justify the experiencer without imposing equivalent obligations on outsiders who cannot independently examine them.

newArguments.title: Specific moral predictions
newArguments.text: Knechtle could replace the weak inference from Christianity's social usefulness to its truth with a comparative prediction. He could specify costly practices that Jesus's teaching would have made unusually likely in the Roman setting, establish how early and broadly those practices appeared, and ask whether rival religious, philosophical, or social influences predict the same pattern equally well. If the pattern is distinctive and independently documented, it offers limited indirect support; contrary Christian conduct, mixed motives, and plausible alternative causes would appropriately reduce that support rather than disappear from the analysis.

finalArgument.thesis: Christianity lacks adequate rational warrant because even established historical and experiential facts do not specifically favor its supernatural explanations over plausible natural alternatives or independently connect reported events to divine agency.
premises: Internal coherence and practical usefulness cannot by themselves establish actuality, because coherent fictions and beneficial institutions may rest on false underlying explanations; truth therefore requires independent evidential support.

Historical reports gain evidential weight from provenance, independence, adverse attestation, and corroboration; however, accurate textual preservation shows transmission fidelity, not that the narrated events actually occurred.
Even a reliably observed extraordinary event would not establish divine agency unless further evidence favored that cause over error, legend, psychological effects, or unknown natural processes.

Because cooperation, sacrifice, hope, and religious desire admit natural and cultural explanations, their compatibility with Christianity provides only weak, nonspecific confirmation without comparative predictive advantage.

Biblical violence, eternal punishment, and forgiveness create unresolved proportional-justice tensions: finite wrongdoing can receive infinite punishment while victims may be excluded, weakening Christianity’s claim to a coherent divine moral character.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, absent independent confirmation that the reported events occurred and evidence discriminating divine agency from error, legend, psychology, or unknown natural causes, Christianity's compatible observations provide inadequate warrant for its supernatural core.

newArguments.title: Likelihood-ratio challenge
newArguments.text: Dillahunty could compare how probable each cited fact would be if Christianity were true with its probability under historical and psychological alternatives. Evidence shared equally by rival explanations has a likelihood ratio near one and therefore contributes little discriminatory weight, even when many observations are accumulated. Distinctive evidence would need to be substantially more expected under Christianity and sufficiently independent to avoid double-counting. This reframing replaces the categorical claim that there is no evidence with the more defensible conclusion that the offered evidence provides little comparative support, directly meeting the cumulative case on probabilistic terms.

newArguments.title: Source-dependence audit
newArguments.text: The con case could turn its general historical criteria into a source-by-source audit of the alleged six resurrection witnesses. For each source, it should identify date, authorship, genre, access to eyewitnesses, theological interests, literary dependence, and any details unlikely to derive from a shared tradition. It could then discount claims that are repeated but not independently attested and compare the residue with ordinary explanations such as memory distortion or legendary development. This would show why numerical multiplicity is not automatically corroboration without dismissing testimony as intrinsically worthless.

newArguments.title: Divine communication prediction
newArguments.text: Hiddenness could be framed as a comparative prediction rather than as a claim about what God is obligated to do. If a loving, communicative God seeks relationship with people, then sincere inquiry should often converge on recognizable access to that God, even though knowledge would not compel worship or loyalty. By contrast, persistent disagreement that tracks culture and remains among nonresistant inquirers is more expected if religions arise through ordinary human processes. The con case could therefore treat hiddenness as positive likelihood evidence against Christianity, while allowing that isolated ambiguity may serve other purposes.

pro.text: God gives us just enough evidence
pro.context: Knechtle used this claim to reconcile divine hiddenness with rational trust, contending that overwhelming manifestation would compromise freely chosen relationship.

con.text: consistent with the facts of reality
con.context: Dillahunty made correspondence with independently supported reality, rather than internal consistency alone, the governing standard for rational Christian belief.
